entries.verbatim: Taking this contribution up involves the following. Claim: the disputes about what agreements meant are treated here as symptoms of underspecified verbal agreements rather than bad faith, and this claim could be wrong; if one flatmate is in fact quietly reneging, written records will surface that instead of fixing it, and the advice would need to change. Proposed application: a written record of any chore agreement (task, standard, deadline), a five-minute standing weekly check-in, weekly rotating task ownership with a swap-before-not-after rule, and a private low-stakes reframe offered to the avoiding friend. These are proposed actions, not established solutions; their uptake depends on all three of you, and especially on the avoidant friend accepting at least a low-stakes version, which cannot be assumed. Proposed test and its relevance: run the arrangement for four weeks and compare the frequency and heat of chore disputes against the previous month; the check-in attendance of the avoidant friend is a second observable. Criticism I accept in advance: written systems can read as bureaucratic and can increase resentment in some households, and if a written record starts being used as evidence in arguments, that is a signal to simplify rather than tighten. Unresolved problems I am flagging: the avoidance may be about something other than chores, in which case chore reform will not touch it and a different conversation would be needed; and if arguments persist but move to another subject, the chores were partly a proxy, which this plan does not address. Scope: this is offered for an ordinary flat-share dispute; it assumes no safety concern and no severe breakdown in the friendship, and it should be dropped if either is present. Revision commitment: after the trial, discard what does not fit rather than defending it, and if the written check fails twice to prevent the same dispute twice, treat the disagreement as about standards or fairness rather than memory and rene

entries.verbatim:
Taking this up means committing to the central reading: the flat's chore conflict is a coordination failure — verbal, memory-held agreements colliding with schedule churn — rather than a character failure of any flatmate, and the disputes are chiefly about scope and standard rather than about who agreed. If the written system is tried and the arguments continue, that reading should be revised before the people are blamed; the failure would then be evidence that the conflict is about something else, such as perceived unfairness of load or the aversiveness of particular tasks, which checklists alone do not touch.

The proposed application carries specific undertakings: define each chore once as a written checklist with scope, completion standard, and frequency; adopt either rotation or, preferably where schedules are erratic, a weekly quota with self-chosen timing; propose the change through the existing written channel rather than a convened meeting; frame it as a four-week trial with a review; and avoid any two-on-one presentation to the avoidant friend.

One part rests on a stated guess: that the avoidance is caused by the conflict itself and will ease once disputes stop. That is not established by the material. If avoidance persists after the disputes subside, or turns out to have another source — workload, health, feeling outnumbered — the prescription for that person changes and calls for a separate, gentler conversation that this account does not supply.

Accepted costs of the proposal: some bureaucratic feel among friends; the asker does the setup work and must keep the sheet current or the system dies; and a rotation means everyone eventually does the disliked tasks, which may itself need renegotiation.

Unresolved: whether the two flatmates, especially the avoidant one, will accept any of it; and whether after a fair trial a flatmate's non-participation would call for the harder conversation about the living arrangement that the account names but does not de

entries.verbatim: Taking this up means acting on a conjecture — that the disputes are standards-and-legitimacy fights rather than memory failures — and being willing to see it fail: if a month of domain ownership with a written floor still produces task-scope arguments ('you didn't really clean it'), the memory-ambiguity diagnosis gains ground and the rival account's checklist deserves the trial instead. It also means committing to the concrete pieces: three or four sized-or-bundled domains, a co-authored one-or-two-line written floor and nothing more, monthly rather than weekly fairness accounting, domain swaps at a short scheduled monthly review, and a first one-on-one conversation with the avoiding friend that carries no proposal — only first pick of a domain and authorship of the floor — accepting that their answer may be 'I just hate chores,' or that the trouble lies outside chores entirely, in which case this plan is beside the point and only the review ritual survives. Two predictions are falsifiable and should be dropped if disconfirmed: that a checklist drafted by the most meticulous flatmate will be read as one side's standard with authority added, and that it will shift disputes into the document's gaps; a checklist trial that reduces arguments without lawyer-fights defeats both. Scope is one flat of three friends, not shared housing in general, and the avoider's avoidance is left as an open question the plan guesses at rather than settles.
